audience: Students with basic programming knowledge learning assembly

progression.localImplementation: Native prose and public intermediate/final CLI checks; remote delivery and enforced instructor policies remain pending

title: Build RSA arithmetic
prerequisites: Unsigned arithmetic, loop invariants and full-width pointers
Preserved registers, nested calls and stack frames
Little-endian word objects and exact memory ownership
learningObjectives: Trace Euclidean remainders and a modular inverse
Use square-and-multiply without discarding product bits
Represent unsigned128-bit inputs with four limbs
Propagate full-product carries and a129th sum bit
Build reduction and modular multiplication with residue invariants
Use every exponent bit and compare with BigInteger.modPow
Distinguish modular arithmetic from RSA encoding schemes

quiz.prompt: Does development status three certify an arithmetic answer?

choices.text: Only for a zero exponent.
No; it marks unfinished work.
Yes, if the low byte happens to match.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
An unfinished return is observable without claiming a completed arithmetic value.

quiz.prompt: Which register pair names the changing Euclidean inputs?

choices.text: The output pointer and stack pointer.
The two low bytes of the original values.
The working copies in t0 and t1.

hints.text: Separate the original arguments from the changing pair.
Keep the first operand in t0 and the second in t1.

quiz.prompt: Why compute the remainder before overwriting the pair?

choices.text: Both old values are still needed by the division.
The result must be written to a string.
Moving a register changes memory byte order.

hints.text: Check the divisor before taking a remainder.
Compute the remainder in t2 before shifting the old divisor into t0.

quiz.prompt: Which value indicates successful gcd completion?

choices.text: The instruction count.
Zero in v1.
Zero in the gcd result for every input.

hints.text: The numerical return and completion indicator have different registers.
Return t0 in v0 and clear v1 without narrowing either saved state or result.

quiz.prompt: What does the gcd alone establish about an inverse?

choices.text: The complete inverse coefficient automatically.
The byte length of an RSA message.
Whether the operands are coprime.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
The coefficient of17 is minus367, equivalent to2753 modulo3120.

quiz.prompt: Why reduce the initial one?

choices.text: Its residue is zero when the modulus is one.
Every exponent is initially one.
A remainder operation increases the exponent width.

hints.text: Handle zero modulus before considering the output.
Reduce both the base and the identity one, then retain the exponent separately.

steps.title: Multiply for a selected exponent bit

quiz.prompt: What selects this multiplication?

choices.text: The number of bytes in the output object.
The current exponent's low bit.
The sign of the modulus address.

hints.text: Test one bit without shifting away the evidence yet.
Mask exponent bit zero and multiply only on the selected path.

steps.title: Advance to the next power of two

quiz.prompt: Why can the last square be skipped?

choices.text: The modulus changes after every multiply.
A square of the base must always be zero.
No remaining exponent bit can select its result.

hints.text: The next exponent bit corresponds to a squared base.
Shift the remaining exponent first, and skip a final square when it becomes zero.

quiz.prompt: When is discarding the upper product bits valid here?

choices.text: After the complete product has been reduced to the32-bit residue.
Before multiplying any two inputs.
Whenever the output address is32-bit aligned.

hints.text: The remainder fits the declared scalar word.
Use one four-byte store after reduction, followed by a status-zero return.

steps.title: Exercise a product with its top bit set

quiz.prompt: Which interpretation does the scalar product require?

choices.text: An address into the output object.
Unsigned64-bit magnitude.
Signed32-bit value.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
The scalar output is one; a signed-remainder substitution fails this case.

quiz.prompt: Why clear the high four words too?

choices.text: The high half is outside the result contract.
Clearing only one byte resets an entire word.
Later partial products add into those columns.

hints.text: Accumulation needs a known initial value in every column.
Clear32 bytes with a four-byte stride, retaining64-bit pointer arithmetic.

steps.title: Begin a row with a fresh carry

quiz.prompt: Which value resets between rows?

choices.text: The incoming carry for the new row.
Every accumulated product column.
The original input object.

hints.text: A row chooses one limb from the first operand.
Load that limb unsigned and reset the inner offset and carry.

quiz.prompt: Which temporary must retain the whole partial sum?

choices.text: The four-byte output slot after its store.
The64-bit accumulator before splitting.
Only the byte pointer.

hints.text: The temporary has both a result limb and a carry.
Store its low32 bits and logically shift the same64-bit value by32 for the carry.

steps.title: Carry through the rest of a row

quiz.prompt: What determines the destination column?

choices.text: The XOR of the input addresses.
The row index alone for every inner iteration.
The sum of the two operand limb indices.

hints.text: The inner loop walks the second operand.
Advance by four bytes and retain the carry until the next column consumes it.

steps.title: Place the row carry and continue

quiz.prompt: What remains when the next row begins?

choices.text: Previously accumulated output limbs.
The old row's incoming carry as the new starting carry.
Only the most recently stored byte.

hints.text: The final row carry belongs beyond the four inner columns.
Store at output plus row offset plus16, then advance the outer offset.

quiz.prompt: How many output bytes must the full-product check compare?

choices.text: Only the first nonzero word.
Thirty-two.
Only the first sixteen.

hints.text: This interface returns an unreduced product.
Retain all eight words and return zero status.

quiz.prompt: Does a correct low half prove the full product?

choices.text: Yes, because multiplication is commutative.
Only if the inputs are aligned.
No; the high half must also be checked.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
High product words and full return addresses participate in the check.

quiz.prompt: Which test recognizes the all-zero modulus?

choices.text: OR all four limbs and test the combined value.
Test the lowest limb alone.
Interpret the output pointer as the modulus.

hints.text: A modulus with low word zero can still be positive.
OR all four modulus limbs before initializing the offset and carry.

quiz.prompt: What does the final carry represent?

choices.text: The sign of either input pointer.
The bit above the stored128-bit sum.
An output byte that should be ignored.

hints.text: Each per-limb temporary can require33 bits.
Use doubleword additions, store the low word and shift by32 for the next carry.

steps.title: Decide whether one subtraction is required

quiz.prompt: When does equality with the modulus require subtraction?

choices.text: Only if the modulus is negative.
Never, because equality is already a reduced residue.
Always, because the residue must be below the modulus.

hints.text: Carry and unsigned comparison are separate reasons to subtract.
Check final carry first; otherwise compare high limbs, including equality.

quiz.prompt: Why is the temporary's sign useful in this subtraction?

choices.text: The limb difference lies in a signed64-bit range with no ambiguity.
All unsigned64-bit differences use their sign as borrow.
A negative address automatically carries into the next limb.

hints.text: Borrow must survive the low-word store.
Subtract the incoming borrow in64 bits and extract its outgoing value before advancing.

quiz.prompt: Why handle modulus one before the bit loop?

choices.text: The object has no readable low limb.
The private integer one would violate that loop's addition precondition.
The exponent becomes negative for modulus one.

hints.text: Zero and one require different public results.
Test all limbs for zero, then recognize one with all three high limbs zero.

quiz.prompt: Which comparison permits the direct copy?

choices.text: Input less than or equal to modulus.
Input address lower than modulus address.
Input strictly less than modulus.

hints.text: Comparison begins at the most significant word.
Copy only on strict input-less-than-modulus; equality follows reduction.

quiz.prompt: What does the private remainder describe?

choices.text: The already consumed binary prefix modulo N.
The count of nonzero input limbs.
The complete256-bit product.

hints.text: Each private object needs all its high limbs initialized.
Zero the remainder and one object, then set the low word of the latter to one.

steps.title: Double the prefix and extract a bit

quiz.prompt: How is a bit index converted to its containing word's byte offset?

choices.text: Use the original bit index as an address.
Divide by32, then multiply by four.
Multiply directly by32.

hints.text: Extract the bit from its containing word.
Divide the index by32 for the word number, multiply by four for bytes, then mask the shifted word.

steps.title: Append each input bit to the remainder

quiz.prompt: Which value must survive a nested call across iterations?

choices.text: Only a discarded product byte.
The old contents of every volatile temporary.
The retained input-bit index.

hints.text: A one bit appends one after doubling the prefix.
Conditionally call modular addition with the private one, then decrement the saved bit index.

steps.title: Copy the completed remainder to the caller

quiz.prompt: Why does the direct-copy path avoid the slow-path restore?

choices.text: It never allocated that frame.
A smaller input has no return address.
Restoring only the low word of sp is sufficient.

hints.text: Publication follows the complete private calculation.
Copy four words and use the supplied slow-path restore only when that frame exists.

quiz.prompt: Which path must restore the reducer's slow frame?

choices.text: Only a path whose result is nonzero.
A path that reached reduce_slow and allocated it.
Every path including the early zero-modulus error.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
Every development path restores exactly the frame it actually allocated.

quiz.prompt: May this entry assume its first operand is already below N?

choices.text: Yes, because it has four limbs.
Yes, whenever its address is aligned.
No; it must establish the residue internally.

hints.text: Do not narrow a multiword zero test.
Combine all four modulus limbs before either operand is read.

steps.title: Retain a private multiplier and reduced addend

quiz.prompt: Which object is shifted destructively?

choices.text: The private multiplier copy.
The caller's read-only multiplier.
The modulus itself.

hints.text: The multiplier will be shifted; retain caller ownership.
Copy it into the frame, initialize R to zero and reduce A into private X.

steps.title: Add for the current multiplier bit

quiz.prompt: Why is the nested result update allowed in place?

choices.text: The stack pointer makes all overlap harmless.
The modular-addition contract explicitly permits that exact alias.
Every public arithmetic output may overlap any input.

hints.text: The low multiplier bit selects the addend.
Update R with addmod(R,X,N,R) only for a one bit, and check nested status.

quiz.prompt: Which bit crosses the doubleword boundary?

choices.text: The high bit of the low half moves upward.
The sign bit is copied into both halves.
The old low bit of the high half.

hints.text: A logical shift needs a transfer between halves.
Move the old high half's bit zero into the low half's bit63.

steps.title: Double the addend for the next bit

quiz.prompt: What invariant relates these three values to the original product?

choices.text: R plus X times Y is congruent to the original product modulo N.
R is always the original first operand.
Y is always the modulus.

hints.text: The addend must match the next multiplier bit's weight.
Double X modulo N after a nonfinal shift and return to the selection test.

quiz.prompt: Which multiplier checks the high-end scan?

choices.text: Only a multiplier whose low byte is odd.
One with only bit127 set.
Only the integer one.

hints.text: The private residue and caller object are separate.
Copy exactly sixteen result bytes, then restore the saved frame.

quiz.prompt: What should completed free-writing grading require?

choices.text: The reference's scratch-register choices.
An exact reference instruction count.
The declared numerical and state contract.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
Equivalent completed implementations agree at the interface despite different traces.

quiz.prompt: How many exponent bits belong to this interface?

choices.text: All128.
Only the lowest32.
Only the number of bits in the output address.

hints.text: An exponent object can have set bits above bit63.
Guard the complete modulus before reading that object or the base.

steps.title: Retain the exponent and reduce both initial values

quiz.prompt: Why use separate temporary output for these calls?

choices.text: The result must share the modulus object.
Their output must be disjoint from input objects.
A pointer always needs32 extra bytes.

hints.text: Both initial values need the same residue invariant.
Reduce base and identity separately, with disjoint temporary output for the identity call.

steps.title: Multiply the result for a one exponent bit

quiz.prompt: Which object changes in this selected multiply?

choices.text: The modulus.
The original caller exponent.
The accumulated result after temporary publication.

hints.text: The public modular-product output is disjoint.
Multiply R and current base into T, check status, then copy T into R.

quiz.prompt: Why test both halves after shifting?

choices.text: Remaining one bits may be entirely in the high half.
The low half stores the modulus.
The address ordering changes after a shift.

hints.text: A zero low half is not a zero128-bit exponent.
Transfer the high half's low bit and test both shifted halves.

steps.title: Prepare the next base and repeat

quiz.prompt: Which value is squared in this right-to-left variant?

choices.text: The original exponent.
The current base.
The accumulated result on every iteration.

hints.text: The two power-loop variants square different state.
For the illustrated right-to-left loop, square the current base into T and copy back.

quiz.prompt: What must a second call be allowed to reuse safely?

choices.text: A hidden cached result for every input.
Only a freshly created simulator session.
Stack and temporary storage with arbitrary previous contents.

hints.text: A later invocation may encounter stale private bytes.
Publish all four words and restore every saved64-bit register before returning.

quiz.prompt: What remains outside the arithmetic lab?

choices.text: Standardized scheme encoding and its complete key-handling behavior.
The low-limb byte order.
The need to retain a carry in multiplication.

hints.text: Identify the function boundary and which state is numerical data.
A modular power is not itself an encryption or signature scheme.
